This is not just unusual; it suggests a different trauma theme than the stated index event.

With Negative Appraisals absent and no threat/appraisal content linking to preventability, this strategy feels weakly grounded relative to the formulation and selected items.

vignette:
Mateo, a 62-year-old surgeon with a reputation for steady hands and an unshakable calm, first sought therapy six months after the accident. He described his life as having split into a "before" and an "after." The "before" was a life of controlled precision, both in the operating theatre and at home with his wife, Sofia. The "after" began on a rainy Tuesday afternoon when a pickup truck ran a red light, T-boning the passenger side of his sedan where Sofia was sitting. The impact was violent, a chaos of screeching metal and shattering glass. For a moment, suspended in the sudden, shocking silence that followed, all he could register was the acrid smell of the deployed airbag and its rough, synthetic texture pressed hard against his cheek. He turned to see Sofia slumped against the door, her eyes closed, and a profound, animal terror seized him-a fear so absolute it felt more real than the fact he was still breathing.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that moment began to intrude on his life with a will of its own. It wasn't a simple recollection; it was a sensory assault. While reviewing patient charts, the memory would force its way into his mind, and he would suddenly feel the ghost of that coarse airbag fabric on his skin, his heart hammering as if the crash were happening all over again. These fragments were so vivid, so much more real than his memory of breakfast that morning, that he found himself pushing them away before the full sequence could unfold, terrified of reliving the moment he thought his wife was dead. This constant effort to block the memory became a full-time job. He began avoiding any news reports that might mention car accidents and would change the channel if a movie showed so much as a screeching tire, a desperate attempt to keep the past from becoming his present.

This internal battle soon bled into his external world. The memory itself made him hyper-aware of potential dangers, and ordinary moments became fraught with threat. After an intrusive image of the crash flashed through his mind one morning, the starchy texture of his surgical scrubs felt abrasive and alien, too similar to the airbag, causing a wave of nausea to rise in him as he prepared for a procedure. The sight of his wife, once a source of comfort, could now trigger a jolt of the same sickening fear from the accident. This connection between his family and the trauma was the most painful. Seeing Sofia laugh with their grandson would bring not joy, but a phantom echo of that terrifying silence in the car, a reminder of what he almost lost.

In response to these triggers, Mateo's world began to shrink. He stopped driving with his wife in the car, insisting she take her own vehicle even for short trips. He gave up the weekend drives they had always enjoyed, one of the many pleasant activities that now felt too risky. At the hospital, a place once his domain, he found himself avoiding the emergency department, unnerved by the imagery of accidents and injuries that were a routine part of the workflow there. He also stopped his daily morning runs, as the physical stress of a rapidly beating heart and shortness of breath felt indistinguishable from the panic of the crash itself. This avoidance, meant to protect him, only seemed to sensitise him further. By constantly scanning his environment for threats-a crumpled car on the side of the road, a texture, the face of a loved one-he was inadvertently keeping the trauma at the forefront of his mind, making him even more likely to be triggered.

His withdrawal had consequences. Sofia felt him pulling away, mistaking his fear-driven avoidance for a lack of affection. The controlled, confident man she married had been replaced by someone quiet and perpetually on edge. The breaking point came when their grandson asked why Grandpa didn't want to play catch in the yard anymore. Mateo, ambushed by a wave of guilt and the memory of the accident, couldn't answer. He saw in that moment the life he was sacrificing to his fear. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a simple, desperate question: how could he learn to live in the "after" without losing everything, and everyone, he had fought so hard to survive for?
